questions.title: Site of action of Omeprazole is:
questions.question: Site of action of Omeprazole is:

explanations.A: Active H and Cl cotransport is not the target of omeprazole; gastric acid secretion is driven by the H+/K+-ATPase, not by a cotransport mechanism of this kind.
explanations.B: Cl/HCO3 exchange describes a different transport process, not the parietal cell proton pump that omeprazole targets.
explanations.C: The site of action of omeprazole is the H+/K+-ATPase (the "proton pump") of the gastric parietal cell, the final common enzymatic step of acid secretion into the gastric lumen. Omeprazole irreversibly inhibits this pump, which is why proton pump inhibitors achieve more complete and longer-lasting acid suppression than drugs acting earlier in the secretory pathway, such as H2-receptor blockers. Recognising the H+/K+-ATPase as omeprazole’s specific molecular target, rather than the Na/K pump or a cotransport or exchange mechanism, is the fact this question tests.
explanations.D: The Na/K pump is a different ion transporter, present in essentially all cells, and is not the specific parietal cell target that omeprazole inhibits.

questions.title: The following anti-emetic drug is useful in treatment of motion sickness:
questions.question: The following anti-emetic drug is useful in treatment of motion sickness:

explanations.A: Dimenhydrinate, an H1-antihistamine with central anticholinergic activity, is the classic drug of choice for preventing and treating the nausea and vomiting of motion sickness, since it blocks the histaminergic and cholinergic transmission along the vestibular pathway that drives motion-triggered vomiting. This vestibular mechanism is different from the chemoreceptor-trigger-zone dopamine blockade used by antiemetics aimed at chemotherapy- or drug-induced vomiting, which is why dimenhydrinate specifically, rather than a dopamine antagonist, is favoured for motion sickness. Recognising this vestibular, antihistamine-based mechanism is the fact tested here.
explanations.B: Chlorpromazine, a dopamine D2 antagonist, targets the chemoreceptor trigger zone rather than the vestibular pathway that drives motion sickness, so it is not the preferred agent here.
explanations.C: Haloperidol, another dopamine D2 antagonist, similarly targets the chemoreceptor trigger zone rather than the vestibular mechanism of motion sickness.
explanations.D: Metoclopramide’s D2-antagonist, prokinetic mechanism targets the chemoreceptor trigger zone and gut motility, not the vestibular pathway that drives motion sickness.

questions.title: The following drug has both anti-emetic and prokinetic effects:
questions.question: The following drug has both anti-emetic and prokinetic effects:

explanations.A: Hyoscine is an anticholinergic used for motion sickness and GI spasm, but it lacks the prokinetic effect that defines this dual-action question.
explanations.B: Metoclopramide is a dopamine D2-receptor antagonist that blocks D2 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone for its antiemetic effect, and separately enhances gastric motility and emptying for its prokinetic effect. This combination of a genuine antiemetic action with a genuine prokinetic action is unusual among GI drugs, most of which have only one or the other property, which is exactly why metoclopramide is the answer to a question asking for both effects together. This dual action is also what makes it useful in diabetic gastroparesis, where delayed gastric emptying needs a prokinetic rather than just an antiemetic.
explanations.C: Dimenhydrinate is an antihistamine antiemetic without a prokinetic effect on gastric motility.
explanations.D: Chlorpromazine is a dopamine antagonist antiemetic but is not known for a clinically useful prokinetic effect on gastric emptying.

questions.title: The following purgative interferes with absorption of fat-soluble vitamins:
questions.question: The following purgative interferes with absorption of fat-soluble vitamins:

explanations.A: Liquid paraffin, a lubricant/physical purgative, is not absorbed itself but coats the stool and, with chronic use, interferes with the absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K, which dissolve into and are lost with it rather than being absorbed across the gut mucosa. This risk is a well-recognised limitation of long-term liquid paraffin use, distinguishing it from the other purgative types listed, whose primary mechanisms (bulk formation, osmotic pull, or mucosal irritation) do not directly interfere with fat-soluble vitamin absorption in this way. Recognising liquid paraffin as the purgative with this specific malabsorption risk is the fact tested here.
explanations.B: Methyl cellulose, a bulk-forming agent, works by increasing stool bulk and does not carry the specific fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption risk of a lubricant purgative.
explanations.C: Magnesium sulphate, an osmotic purgative, draws water into the lumen and does not interfere with fat-soluble vitamin absorption the way a lubricant purgative does.
explanations.D: Lactulose, an osmotic purgative, works by drawing water into the colon and does not carry the fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption risk specific to liquid paraffin.

questions.title: All of the following are used in treatment of diarrhoea EXCEPT:
questions.question: All of the following are used in treatment of diarrhoea EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Kaolin, an adsorbent, genuinely is used in the treatment of diarrhoea, so it is not the exception.
explanations.B: Neostigmine is a cholinesterase inhibitor that increases cholinergic transmission, which raises gut motility and secretion; it would worsen, not treat, diarrhoea, which is exactly why it is the exception among these options. The genuine treatments for diarrhoea act by adsorbing toxins, replacing lost fluid, or slowing gut motility through an opioid-receptor mechanism, all of which are the opposite direction from what a cholinergic stimulant like neostigmine does. This is the point this question is testing.
explanations.C: Oral rehydration solution genuinely is used in the treatment of diarrhoea, replacing lost fluid and electrolytes, so it is not the exception.
explanations.D: Loperamide, an antimotility opioid derivative, genuinely is used in the treatment of diarrhoea, so it is not the exception.

questions.title: The following is a mucosal protective agent that is effective in treatment of peptic ulcer, but produces black coloration of mouth cavity and faeces:
questions.question: The following is a mucosal protective agent that is effective in treatment of peptic ulcer, but produces black coloration of mouth cavity and faeces:

explanations.A: Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor, not a mucosal protective agent, and does not cause black staining of the mouth or faeces.
explanations.B: Carbenoxolone is a mucosal protective agent historically used in peptic ulcer treatment, but it is not known for the specific black-staining side effect this question describes.
explanations.C: Colloidal bismuth is a mucosal protective agent effective in peptic ulcer treatment, forming a protective coating over the ulcer base. A well-known, harmless side effect of colloidal bismuth is black discoloration of the mouth cavity and of the faeces, caused by the formation of bismuth sulfide in the gut. Recognising this characteristic, benign black-staining side effect is the fact this question tests, and it should not be mistaken for gastrointestinal bleeding.
explanations.D: Misoprostol, a prostaglandin analogue, is used to prevent NSAID-induced ulcers but is not a mucosal protective agent associated with black staining.

questions.title: Which of the following is a proton pump inhibitor effective in treatment of peptic ulcer:
questions.question: Which of the following is a proton pump inhibitor effective in treatment of peptic ulcer:

explanations.A: Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor, irreversibly blocking the H+/K+-ATPase (the proton pump) of the gastric parietal cell, the final common step in acid secretion. This mechanism gives proton pump inhibitors the most complete and long-lasting suppression of gastric acid secretion among the available anti-secretory drug classes, which is why omeprazole is effective in the treatment of peptic ulcer disease. Recognising omeprazole as a proton pump inhibitor, distinct from the H2-receptor blockers, anticholinergics and prostaglandin analogues among the other options, is the fact tested here.
explanations.B: Ranitidine is an H2-receptor antagonist, not a proton pump inhibitor.
explanations.C: Pirenzepine is a selective M1-anticholinergic, not a proton pump inhibitor.
explanations.D: Misoprostol is a prostaglandin E1 analogue used for NSAID-ulcer prophylaxis, not a proton pump inhibitor.

questions.title: The drug useful to promote healing of duodenal ulcer is:
questions.question: The drug useful to promote healing of duodenal ulcer is:

explanations.A: Sodium citrate is not a drug used to promote duodenal ulcer healing.
explanations.B: Famotidine, an H2-receptor antagonist, is useful to promote healing of duodenal ulcer by reducing gastric acid secretion through blockade of histamine H2 receptors on the parietal cell. This acid-suppressing action allows the mucosal defect to heal over the standard treatment course, in the same way as the other H2 blockers, and is a core, well-established use of this drug class. Recognising famotidine as an H2 blocker used for duodenal ulcer healing is the fact tested here.
explanations.C: Terfenadine is a peripheral H1-antihistamine used for allergic conditions, unrelated to duodenal ulcer healing.
explanations.D: Ondansetron is a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist antiemetic, unrelated to duodenal ulcer healing.

questions.title: Ranitidine produces which of the following:
questions.question: Ranitidine produces which of the following:

explanations.A: Ranitidine does not block M1 receptors; that is the mechanism of a selective anticholinergic such as pirenzepine.
explanations.B: Ranitidine does not block H1 receptors; H1 blockade is the mechanism of antihistamines such as terfenadine, not of ranitidine.
explanations.C: Ranitidine produces blockade of histamine H2 receptors on the gastric parietal cell, reducing gastric acid secretion. This H2-receptor mechanism is shared by the whole drug class (cimetidine, famotidine, nizatidine) and is distinct from the H1-antihistamine, M1-anticholinergic, and direct acid-neutralising mechanisms of the other options. Recognising H2-receptor blockade as ranitidine’s specific mechanism is the fact this question tests.
explanations.D: Ranitidine does not act by direct acid neutralisation; that mechanism belongs to antacids, not to an H2-receptor blocker.

questions.title: Drugs useful in eradication of H. pylori include the following EXCEPT:
questions.question: Drugs useful in eradication of H. pylori include the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Amoxicillin genuinely is used in H. pylori eradication regimens, so it is not the exception.
explanations.B: Clarithromycin genuinely is used in H. pylori eradication regimens, so it is not the exception.
explanations.C: Rifampicin is an antitubercular antibiotic and plays no role in standard Helicobacter pylori eradication regimens, which is why it is the exception among these options. The genuine antibiotics used for H. pylori eradication, in various combination regimens with a proton pump inhibitor, are amoxicillin, clarithromycin, metronidazole and tetracycline. Excluding rifampicin from this list, despite it being a familiar antibacterial, is the point this question is testing.
explanations.D: Tetracycline genuinely is used in H. pylori eradication regimens (particularly bismuth-based quadruple therapy), so it is not the exception.

questions.title: Drugs useful in maintenance treatment to prevent ulcer relapse include:
questions.question: Drugs useful in maintenance treatment to prevent ulcer relapse include:

explanations.A: Aspirin is not used in maintenance treatment to prevent ulcer relapse; it is in fact a recognised cause of gastric mucosal injury and ulceration.
explanations.B: Ranitidine, an H2-receptor antagonist, is used in maintenance treatment to prevent ulcer relapse once an ulcer has healed, continuing to suppress gastric acid secretion at a lower dose than the initial healing course. This maintenance role reflects the tendency of peptic ulcers to recur once acid-suppressing treatment is stopped, particularly in patients with ongoing risk factors, and H2 blockers are a standard option for this purpose. Recognising ranitidine’s maintenance-therapy role, distinct from aspirin, sodium bicarbonate or metronidazole, is the fact tested here.
explanations.C: Sodium bicarbonate is a short-acting systemic antacid, not a drug used for long-term maintenance therapy to prevent ulcer relapse.
explanations.D: Metronidazole is an antimicrobial used in H. pylori eradication regimens, not a drug used specifically for maintenance therapy to prevent ulcer relapse.

questions.title: All of the following are true about cimetidine EXCEPT:
questions.question: All of the following are true about cimetidine EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Cimetidine genuinely is useful in duodenal ulcer treatment, so this true statement is not the exception.
explanations.B: Cimetidine genuinely may cause mental confusion, particularly in elderly patients, so this true statement is not the exception.
explanations.C: Cimetidine is an H2-receptor antagonist, not an H1-receptor antagonist, which is why calling it an H1-receptor antagonist is the false statement among these options and the exception the question asks for. Its actual mechanism, blockade of histamine H2 receptors on the gastric parietal cell, is what gives it its acid-suppressing effect, and it shares this H2 mechanism with the rest of its drug class (ranitidine, famotidine, nizatidine), not the H1 mechanism of a classic antihistamine. Confusing the two histamine receptor subtypes is a common error this question is designed to catch.
explanations.D: Cimetidine genuinely may cause hepatic dysfunction as an adverse effect, so this true statement is not the exception.

questions.title: All the following may cause diarrhoea as a side effect EXCEPT:
questions.question: All the following may cause diarrhoea as a side effect EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Digoxin genuinely can cause diarrhoea as a side effect, so this true statement is not the exception.
explanations.B: Codeine, an opioid, does not cause diarrhoea as a side effect; through its opioid receptor-mediated reduction of gut motility, codeine instead classically causes constipation, the opposite direction of bowel disturbance from the other options. This is exactly why codeine is the exception among a list of drugs that cause diarrhoea, since its recognised GI side effect works in the reverse direction. Recognising this reversal is the point this question is testing.
explanations.C: Misoprostol genuinely can cause diarrhoea as a side effect, through its prostaglandin-driven increase in intestinal motility and secretion, so this true statement is not the exception.
explanations.D: Metformin genuinely can cause diarrhoea as a common side effect, so this true statement is not the exception.

questions.title: Loperamide is:
questions.question: Loperamide is:

explanations.A: Loperamide is not an analgesic anti-pyretic; that description belongs to drugs such as paracetamol or NSAIDs, not to loperamide.
explanations.B: Loperamide is not classified as an anti-tussive (cough suppressant), even though it is chemically related to the opioid analgesic meperidine.
explanations.C: Loperamide is an anti-diarrhoeal agent, acting on opioid receptors in the bowel wall to slow gut motility. It is chemically related to the strong opioid analgesic meperidine, but its poor penetration of the central nervous system at normal doses spares it from significant central opioid effects, which is what allows it to be classified simply as an anti-diarrhoeal rather than as a systemic opioid analgesic. This distinction between its peripheral gut action and the central effects of related opioids is the fact this question tests.
explanations.D: Loperamide is not an anti-emetic; its action is on gut motility to treat diarrhoea, not on the vomiting pathway.

questions.title: Drugs useful to control vomiting include the following EXCEPT:
questions.question: Drugs useful to control vomiting include the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Chlorpromazine genuinely is used to control vomiting through dopamine D2 receptor blockade, so this true statement is not the exception.
explanations.B: Domperidone genuinely is used to control vomiting through peripheral dopamine D2 receptor blockade, so this true statement is not the exception.
explanations.C: Ondansetron genuinely is used to control vomiting through 5-HT3 receptor blockade, so this true statement is not the exception.
explanations.D: Apomorphine is a dopamine agonist that stimulates the chemoreceptor trigger zone and induces, rather than controls, vomiting, historically used as an emetic in the management of poisoning. This is the opposite pharmacological direction from the genuine antiemetics chlorpromazine, domperidone and ondansetron, all of which block rather than stimulate their respective vomiting-pathway receptors. This is exactly why apomorphine is the exception among these options, and the answer to this question.

questions.title: Ondansetron is useful in treatment of:
questions.question: Ondansetron is useful in treatment of:

explanations.A: Ondansetron, a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist, is useful in the treatment of vomiting induced by cancer therapy (chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting), its primary and best-established indication. It blocks serotonin (5-HT3) receptors both centrally in the chemoreceptor trigger zone and peripherally on vagal afferents in the gut, the site where chemotherapy triggers much of its emetogenic signal. Recognising chemotherapy-induced vomiting, rather than motion sickness or pregnancy-related vomiting, as ondansetron’s classic indication is the fact this question tests.
explanations.B: Ondansetron is not the standard treatment for vomiting of pregnancy, where other agents are generally preferred first-line.
explanations.C: Ondansetron is not the standard treatment for motion sickness, which instead responds better to a vestibular-targeting antihistamine such as dimenhydrinate.
explanations.D: Ondansetron is not the standard treatment for acute migraine, whose treatment targets the headache mechanism rather than the chemotherapy-triggered vomiting pathway.

questions.title: Treatment of diarrhoea includes use of the following EXCEPT:
questions.question: Treatment of diarrhoea includes use of the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Antimicrobial agents genuinely are used in the treatment of diarrhoea when an infective cause is identified, so this true statement is not the exception.
explanations.B: Fluid replacement genuinely is a core component of diarrhoea treatment, so this true statement is not the exception.
explanations.C: Muscarinic agonists are not used in the treatment of diarrhoea; stimulating muscarinic receptors would increase, not decrease, gut motility and secretion, worsening rather than treating diarrhoea. This is the opposite direction from the genuine treatments — antimicrobial agents, fluid replacement, and antimotility drugs such as loperamide — which is exactly why muscarinic agonists are the exception among these options. Recognising that a cholinergic stimulant would worsen diarrhoea is the point this question is testing.
explanations.D: Loperamide genuinely is used in the treatment of diarrhoea, so this true statement is not the exception.

questions.title: Which of the following is not an anti-diarrhoeal agent:
questions.question: Which of the following is not an anti-diarrhoeal agent:

explanations.A: Kaolin genuinely is an anti-diarrhoeal adsorbent agent, so it is not the answer to this "not an anti-diarrhoeal agent" question.
explanations.B: Diphenoxylate genuinely is an anti-diarrhoeal opioid-derivative agent, so it is not the answer to this "not an anti-diarrhoeal agent" question.
explanations.C: Loperamide genuinely is an anti-diarrhoeal opioid-derivative agent, so it is not the answer to this "not an anti-diarrhoeal agent" question.
explanations.D: Indapamide is a thiazide-like diuretic used for hypertension, entirely unrelated to gastrointestinal motility, which is why it is not an anti-diarrhoeal agent at all, unlike kaolin, diphenoxylate and loperamide. Its mechanism acts on renal sodium and water handling, not on gut secretion or motility, so it has no role in diarrhoea treatment. Recognising indapamide as a diuretic rather than a GI drug is the fact this question tests.

questions.title: Direct spasmolytics include the following drugs EXCEPT:
questions.question: Direct spasmolytics include the following drugs EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Aminophylline genuinely is a direct (musculotropic) spasmolytic, acting on smooth muscle independent of receptor blockade, so it is not the exception.
explanations.B: Atropine sulfate is an anticholinergic drug, working by blocking muscarinic receptors, not by the direct musculotropic action that defines the "direct spasmolytics" category. This distinction is exactly why atropine, despite genuinely relieving GI spasm, is classed separately from mebeverine, papaverine and aminophylline, all of which act directly on smooth muscle rather than through receptor blockade. Recognising this direct-versus-anticholinergic distinction is the point this question is testing.
explanations.C: Mebeverine genuinely is a direct (musculotropic) spasmolytic, so it is not the exception.
explanations.D: Papaverine genuinely is a direct (musculotropic) spasmolytic, so it is not the exception.

questions.title: Physical purgatives include which of the following:
questions.question: Physical purgatives include which of the following:

explanations.A: Dioctyl sodium sulphosuccinate, a surfactant/stool-softening agent, is classed among the physical purgatives, which act by a lubricating or softening physical mechanism rather than by mucosal irritation. This physical mechanism distinguishes it from the irritant (stimulant) purgatives, such as bisacodyl, castor oil and croton oil, which instead act by directly stimulating the bowel mucosa to increase peristaltic activity. Recognising dioctyl sodium sulphosuccinate’s physical rather than irritant classification is the fact this question tests.
explanations.B: Bisacodyl is classed as an irritant (stimulant) purgative, acting by mucosal stimulation, not among the physical purgatives.
explanations.C: Castor oil is classed as an irritant (stimulant) purgative, acting by mucosal stimulation, not among the physical purgatives.
explanations.D: Croton oil is classed as a potent irritant purgative, acting by mucosal stimulation, not among the physical purgatives.

questions.title: Irritant purgatives act by which of the following:
questions.question: Irritant purgatives act by which of the following:

explanations.A: Irritant purgatives increase, not decrease, peristaltic activity; decreasing it would be the opposite of a purgative’s intended laxative effect.
explanations.B: Irritant (stimulant) purgatives act by directly stimulating the bowel mucosa, which increases peristaltic activity and accelerates transit of the bowel contents. This direct mucosal-stimulation mechanism is what distinguishes irritant purgatives such as bisacodyl and castor oil from the physical (lubricant) and osmotic categories, which work instead by softening the stool or drawing in water rather than by directly stimulating peristalsis. Recognising increased peristaltic activity as the irritant purgative mechanism is the fact this question tests.
explanations.C: Decreased faecal surface tension describes a surfactant/stool-softening mechanism, the physical purgative category, not the irritant purgative mechanism.
explanations.D: Bulk-forming describes agents like methyl cellulose that increase stool bulk to trigger reflex peristalsis, a different mechanism from direct mucosal irritation.

questions.question: Purgatives are used in the following conditions EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Purgatives genuinely are used before operations to clear the bowel, so this true statement is not the exception.
explanations.B: Purgatives genuinely are used after anti-helminthic treatment, to help expel dead or paralysed worms from the bowel, so this true statement is not the exception.
explanations.C: Purgatives are contraindicated in gastroenteritis, where the bowel is already acutely inflamed and fluid loss already excessive; adding a purgative would worsen both the inflammation and the dehydration risk rather than help. This is the opposite of the genuine indications for purgative use — before operations, after anti-helminthic treatment, and in oral drug poisoning to hasten elimination — which is exactly why gastroenteritis is the exception among these options. Recognising this contraindication is the point this question is testing.
explanations.D: Purgatives genuinely are used in oral drug poisoning, to hasten elimination of the ingested toxin, so this true statement is not the exception.

questions.title: Dissolution of cholesterol stones in the gall bladder can be achieved by:
questions.question: Dissolution of cholesterol stones in the gall bladder can be achieved by:

explanations.A: Glycolic acid is not the bile acid used for medical dissolution of cholesterol gallstones.
explanations.B: Chenodeoxycholic acid, a bile acid, can dissolve cholesterol gallstones by reducing the cholesterol saturation of bile over weeks to months, offering an alternative to surgery in selected patients with small, radiolucent cholesterol stones and a functioning gall bladder. This works by shifting the balance of bile’s components rather than by any direct chemical reaction on the stone itself, distinguishing it from the other listed acids. Recognising chenodeoxycholic acid as the gallstone-dissolving bile acid is the fact this question tests.
explanations.C: Acetoacetic acid is a ketone body, unrelated to gallstone dissolution therapy.
explanations.D: Acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) is an NSAID, unrelated to gallstone dissolution therapy.

questions.title: Which risk factor is most likely to predispose a patient to the complications of peptic ulcer disease?
questions.question: Which risk factor is most likely to predispose a patient to the complications of peptic ulcer disease?

explanations.A: Obesity is not the risk factor most strongly linked to complications of peptic ulcer disease.
explanations.B: Race, on its own, is not the risk factor most strongly linked to complications of peptic ulcer disease.
explanations.C: Age, on its own, is not the risk factor most strongly linked to complications of peptic ulcer disease.
explanations.D: Helicobacter pylori infection is the risk factor most likely to predispose a patient to the complications of peptic ulcer disease, such as bleeding and perforation, through its direct mucosal injury and chronic inflammatory effect on the gastric and duodenal lining. This direct causal mechanism makes H. pylori infection a stronger and more specific predictor of complications than the more general demographic factors of obesity, race or age. Recognising H. pylori as the dominant risk factor here is the fact this question tests.

questions.title: Castor oil is classified as which type of laxative?
questions.question: Castor oil is classified as which type of laxative?

explanations.A: Castor oil is not a lubricating laxative; that category describes agents such as liquid paraffin, which coat rather than stimulate the bowel.
explanations.B: Castor oil is not an anthraquinone laxative; anthraquinones are a distinct chemical class of stimulant laxative (such as senna), not the fatty-acid-derived mechanism of castor oil.
explanations.C: Castor oil is classified as an irritant (stimulant) laxative. In the small intestine it is hydrolysed to ricinoleic acid, which directly irritates the bowel mucosa and stimulates increased peristaltic activity, producing a relatively rapid purgative effect. This direct mucosal-stimulation mechanism places castor oil in the same irritant category as bisacodyl and croton oil, distinct from the lubricating, anthraquinone or stool-softening categories among the other options.
explanations.D: Castor oil is not a stool-softening laxative; that category describes surfactant agents such as dioctyl sodium sulphosuccinate, a different mechanism from castor oil’s mucosal irritation.

questions.title: Which of the following antacids can be complicated with diarrhoea?
questions.question: Which of the following antacids can be complicated with diarrhoea?

explanations.A: Aluminium hydroxide characteristically causes constipation, not diarrhoea, the opposite bowel effect from a magnesium antacid.
explanations.B: Magnesium trisilicate, a magnesium-containing antacid, can be complicated by diarrhoea, since magnesium salts draw water into the bowel lumen in the same way that magnesium hydroxide itself is used deliberately as an osmotic laxative. This osmotic, water-drawing effect is the mechanism behind magnesium antacids’ characteristic diarrhoea side effect, in contrast to the constipating effect of aluminium-containing antacids. Recognising magnesium trisilicate’s diarrhoea risk, and the reason for it, is the fact this question tests.
explanations.C: Calcium carbonate more typically causes constipation, and can also cause milk-alkali syndrome with excessive use, rather than the diarrhoea characteristic of magnesium salts.
explanations.D: Sodium bicarbonate is a systemic antacid whose main risks are metabolic alkalosis and acid rebound, not the osmotic diarrhoea characteristic of magnesium salts.

questions.question: Cimetidine:

options.B: Provides direct protective effect on gastric mucosa

explanations.A: Cimetidine is an H2-receptor blocker, not an H1-receptor blocker, so this option misstates its receptor target.
explanations.B: Cimetidine does not provide a direct protective effect on the gastric mucosa; its action is acid-suppressive, through H2-receptor blockade, not mucosal-protective like sucralfate or bismuth.
explanations.C: Cimetidine can be complicated by gynaecomastia, a recognised adverse effect arising from its weak anti-androgenic activity, which can cause breast tissue enlargement in male patients on prolonged treatment. This endocrine side effect is one of cimetidine’s more distinctive adverse effects, alongside its cytochrome P450 drug interactions, and is much less prominent with the newer H2 blockers such as famotidine or ranitidine. Recognising gynaecomastia as a genuine cimetidine complication is the fact this question tests.
explanations.D: Cimetidine inhibits, rather than accelerates, the hepatic metabolism of other drugs, through its cytochrome P450-inhibiting effect, the opposite of what this option claims.

questions.title: H. pylori infection can be eradicated by a two-week course of:
questions.question: H. pylori infection can be eradicated by a two-week course of:

explanations.A: Helicobacter pylori infection can be eradicated by a two-week course of a proton pump inhibitor such as omeprazole together with the antibiotics clarithromycin and amoxicillin, the classic triple therapy regimen. This combination pairs acid suppression, which improves antibiotic efficacy and symptom relief, with two antibiotics chosen for their activity against H. pylori and their tolerability together, over a fixed treatment course. Recognising this specific PPI-clarithromycin-amoxicillin combination as standard triple therapy is the fact this question tests.
explanations.B: Clarithromycin, amoxicillin and metronidazole together, without a proton pump inhibitor, is not the standard triple therapy regimen described here.
explanations.C: Omeprazole plus clarithromycin alone, without a second antibiotic, is an incomplete regimen compared with the standard three-drug triple therapy.
explanations.D: Omeprazole plus amoxicillin alone, without a second antibiotic such as clarithromycin, is an incomplete regimen compared with the standard three-drug triple therapy.

questions.title: All of the following drugs can be used in treatment of peptic ulcer, EXCEPT:
questions.question: All of the following drugs can be used in treatment of peptic ulcer, EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Sucralfate, a mucosal protectant, genuinely is used in the treatment of peptic ulcer, so it is not the exception.
explanations.B: Pirenzepine, a selective M1-anticholinergic that reduces acid secretion, genuinely is used in the treatment of peptic ulcer, so it is not the exception.
explanations.C: Bismuth salts, mucosal protectants, genuinely are used in the treatment of peptic ulcer, so they are not the exception.
explanations.D: Prednisolone, a corticosteroid, is not used in the treatment of peptic ulcer; by suppressing prostaglandin synthesis and impairing mucosal defence, corticosteroids are instead a recognised risk factor for causing ulcers, the opposite role from sucralfate, pirenzepine or bismuth salts. This is exactly why prednisolone is the exception among these options, and the answer to this question. Recognising corticosteroids as an ulcer-causing, rather than ulcer-treating, drug class is the point being tested.

questions.title: Which one of the following drugs is NOT a laxative agent?
questions.question: Which one of the following drugs is NOT a laxative agent?

explanations.A: Methyl cellulose genuinely is a laxative agent (bulk-forming), so it is not the answer to this "NOT a laxative" question.
explanations.B: Diphenoxylate is an antidiarrhoeal opioid-derivative drug, not a laxative agent at all; it slows gut motility to treat diarrhoea, the opposite pharmacological direction from a laxative, which is exactly why it is the drug that is NOT a laxative among these options. Recognising diphenoxylate’s antidiarrhoeal, rather than laxative, classification is the fact this question tests. Confusing the two opposite-acting drug categories is exactly the error this question is designed to catch.
explanations.C: Liquid paraffin genuinely is a laxative agent (lubricant/physical), so it is not the answer to this "NOT a laxative" question.
explanations.D: Lactulose genuinely is a laxative agent (osmotic), so it is not the answer to this "NOT a laxative" question.
